I don't even know where to begin, so let me just start with the beginning, which was, in fairness, fine. We were sat within ten minutes of our reservation time, which for a Saturday night is apparently the best service you can hope for these days, so truly, bravo.

The bread basket arrived promptly. I have no notes on the bread basket. The bread basket, if I'm being honest, was the high point of the evening, and I don't say that sarcastically — the sourdough was genuinely excellent, and I'm not the sort of person who says something is excellent when I don't mean it, unlike, apparently, whoever trained our waiter.

Our waiter, whose name I never caught because he introduced himself once, at the beginning, in the specific tone of someone who has said his own name four thousand times and has grown to resent it, took our drink order and then did not return for what my phone's timestamp later confirmed was 23 minutes. Twenty-three minutes for two glasses of house wine. I am not a difficult person. I did not complain at the 10-minute mark, or the 15-minute mark. By the 20-minute mark I'll admit I was watching the door he'd disappeared through with the focus of a person watching a kettle that refuses to boil.

When the wine did arrive, he informed us, with what I can only describe as real enthusiasm, that the kitchen was 'running a little behind tonight.' A little behind turned out to mean 55 minutes for two entrees at a restaurant that was maybe two-thirds full. I don't want to be the kind of diner who complains about wait times — restaurants have bad nights, kitchens get slammed, I've worked in food service, I get it — but I also don't think 'I get it' obligates me to sit there in complete silence pretending the bread basket alone constitutes a meal.

The food, when it came, was not bad. I want to be fair here, because I do think a review should be fair, and it would not be fair to say the food was bad. It also would not be accurate to say it was good, exactly. It was food. It arrived. It was warm, mostly. My risotto had the specific gluey consistency of something that had been made correctly forty minutes ago and then held under a heat lamp while the kitchen apologized to several other tables in sequence.

Here is the part that actually prompted this review, though, rather than just a mild grumble I'd have forgotten by Monday: the bill. Our itemized check listed two glasses of the 'Reserve' Cabernet at $22 each, which is not what we ordered — we ordered the house red, which the menu lists at $11 a glass. When I mentioned this to our waiter (finally located, post-meal, with considerably more urgency than during the wine drought earlier), he said, and I'm paraphrasing only slightly, that the system 'sometimes does that' and that he'd 'get it fixed,' before returning eleven minutes later with a revised check that had corrected the wine but somehow now also included a $14 'plating fee' that had not been on the original check at all and appears nowhere on the printed menu.

I want to be clear that I am not accusing anyone of doing this on purpose. I don't think there's a secret plan at this restaurant to quietly upcharge distracted diners at the end of a long, understaffed Saturday night. I think it's more likely just chaos — an overwhelmed staff, a POS system nobody's been properly trained on, a kitchen in the weeds. That's a staffing and management problem, not a diner-scamming problem, and I want to be precise about which one I'm describing, because I think it matters.

Would I go back? Honestly, maybe. The bread was good. The bones of the menu looked promising even if execution was, let's say, aspirational tonight. But if I do go back and a single item on my check doesn't match what I actually ordered a second time, that's the last time, full stop, and I'll be the guy leaving the review that starts with 'I really wanted to like this place.'

Two stars, mostly for the bread.
